title: Unlabeled Button or Link
desc: A button or link does not have an accessible name. Screen readers announce it as "button" or "link" with no context, so users cannot tell what it does.
rem: Add a visible label or an aria-label attribute that describes what the control does. For example, a close button inside a modal should say "Close" or "Close dialog", not just show an X icon.

title: Focus Not Moved When New Content Opens
desc: When a modal, dialog, or drawer opens, keyboard focus stays where it was. Screen reader and keyboard users cannot easily reach the new content.
rem: Move focus to the first element inside the new content when it opens. Use tabindex="-1" on a heading if the first focusable element comes later. Trap focus inside while it is open, and return focus to the trigger button when it closes.

title: Focus Indicator Missing or Not Visible
desc: Keyboard users cannot see which element is focused. The default focus outline may be removed, or the custom focus style is too faint to see clearly.
rem: Make sure every keyboard-focusable element shows a clear focus outline. Do not set outline: none without providing a visible custom focus style. The focus indicator must have at least a 3:1 contrast ratio against nearby colors.

title: Element Not Keyboard Accessible
desc: The control can only be used with a mouse. Keyboard users cannot focus or activate it. Custom elements built with div or span also lack a role, so screen readers do not know what the control is.
rem: Use native HTML elements like button or a whenever possible — they are keyboard accessible and have built-in roles. If a custom element must be used, add tabindex="0", an appropriate ARIA role, and keyboard event handlers for Enter and Space.

title: Text Contrast Too Low
desc: Text does not have enough contrast against its background. People with low vision or color blindness may not be able to read it.
rem: Change the text color, background color, or both so the contrast ratio is at least 4.5:1. Use a color contrast checker tool to verify.

title: Non-text Contrast Too Low
desc: Icons, form input borders, or UI component edges do not have enough contrast against nearby colors. People with low vision may not be able to see or identify them.
rem: Update the color of the element so it has at least a 3:1 contrast ratio against the colors next to it.

title: Alt Text Missing, Wrong, or Unnecessary
desc: An image has no alt text, has alt text that does not describe the image's purpose, or has alt text that repeats nearby visible text.
rem: Decide if the image carries meaning or is purely decorative. Meaningful images need short, descriptive alt text that explains the purpose. Decorative images should use alt="" so screen readers skip them.

title: Control Label Describes Appearance, Not Purpose
desc: A control's accessible name describes how it looks rather than what it does. For example, a button labeled "magnifying glass icon" should instead say "Search".
rem: Write labels that describe the action or destination of the control, not its visual appearance. Change labels like "arrow icon" to "Next page" or "Search icon" to "Search".

title: No Skip Link
desc: There is no skip link at the top of the page. Keyboard users must tab through all navigation links on every page before reaching the main content.
rem: Add a "Skip to main content" link as the first focusable element on the page. Make it visible when focused, and have it move focus to the start of the main content area.

title: Skip Link Not Visible When Focused
desc: A skip link exists but is hidden from sighted keyboard users. When a keyboard user tabs to it, nothing appears on screen.
rem: Make the skip link appear on screen when it receives keyboard focus. It can be hidden off-screen by default, but must become visible when focused.

title: Heading Structure Incorrect
desc: Text that looks like a heading is not marked as one, or heading levels skip numbers (for example, jumping from h1 to h3). Screen reader users navigate pages by headings, so a broken structure makes it hard to find content.
rem: Use h1–h6 elements for all section titles. Do not skip levels — each sub-section should use the next heading level down. Do not use heading elements just to make text larger or bolder.

title: No H1 on the Page
desc: The page has no h1 heading. The h1 is the main title of the page and helps screen reader users understand where they are.
rem: Add a single h1 element to each page that describes the page's main topic. All other headings should follow in order below it.

title: Asterisk for Required Fields Not Explained
desc: The form uses asterisks (*) to mark required fields, but the meaning of the asterisk is never explained. Some users may not know what it means.
rem: Add a note at the top of the form that explains the asterisk, such as "Fields marked with * are required." Also mark required fields programmatically using the required or aria-required attribute.

title: Form Errors Not Linked to Their Fields
desc: When a form shows an error message, screen readers do not announce it because it is not programmatically linked to the input field.
rem: Use aria-describedby to connect the error message to its input field. When errors appear, move keyboard focus to the first field with an error so all users know where to fix the problem.

title: No Status Message After Action
desc: After a user action such as submitting a form or loading results, nothing is announced to screen reader users. They do not know if the action worked.
rem: Use role="status" or aria-live="polite" on a container that receives the result message. This lets screen readers announce updates without moving focus. Only use aria-live="assertive" or role="alert" for urgent messages.

title: ARIA Used Incorrectly
desc: ARIA attributes are applied incorrectly. Common problems: aria-hidden is placed on a focusable element, role="alert" is used for routine messages, or ARIA roles conflict with the element's native behavior.
rem: Follow the ARIA specification closely. Never put aria-hidden on an element that is focusable or contains focusable children. Use role="alert" only for urgent, time-sensitive messages — use aria-live="polite" for everything else.

title: Color Is the Only Visual Indicator
desc: Information is communicated using color alone. For example, a required field is highlighted in red but has no other indicator. People who are colorblind or cannot see colors will miss this information.
rem: Always pair color with a second visual indicator — such as an underline, bold text, an icon, or a text label. Make sure any state changes are also communicated to assistive technology.

title: Zoom or Pinch-to-Zoom Disabled
desc: The page prevents users from zooming in using a browser or pinch gesture. People with low vision rely on zooming to read content.
rem: Remove user-scalable="no" from the viewport meta tag. Do not set maximum-scale below 2. Allow users to zoom freely.

title: Form Field Missing a Label
desc: A form field has no visible label, or its label is not programmatically linked to the field. Placeholder text disappears when the user starts typing and is not a substitute for a proper label.
rem: Give every form field a visible label element that describes what to enter. Link the label to the input using matching for and id attributes. Avoid using placeholder text as the only label.

title: Hidden Content Still Readable by Screen Readers
desc: Content that is visually hidden (such as a closed dropdown or collapsed panel) is still readable by screen readers. Users may hear content that seems to have no context.
rem: Use display: none or visibility: hidden to hide content from both visual and screen reader users. Or use aria-hidden="true" on content that should be invisible to screen readers. Make sure the chosen method actually hides the content from assistive technology.

title: Text Spacing Too Tight
desc: The page does not support minimum text spacing. When users apply custom spacing through browser settings, content breaks or becomes unreadable.
rem: Design and code so the page still works with these values applied: line height at least 1.5× the font size, paragraph spacing at least 2× the font size, letter spacing at least 0.12× the font size, word spacing at least 0.16× the font size.

title: Accessible Name Does Not Match Visible Label
desc: A control's accessible name is different from its visible text label. Voice input users speak the visible label to activate the control, but it does not match what the control is actually named.
rem: Make sure the accessible name starts with or contains the visible label text. Remove aria-label values that replace the visible text — let the visible text serve as the accessible name.

title: ARIA Tabs Pattern
desc: The component uses ARIA tabs, which require arrow key navigation that many users do not expect. ARIA tab patterns are easy to break and hard to implement correctly.
rem: Consider replacing ARIA tabs with a simpler pattern. Accordion, links, or a button-panel structure often provide the same content without the added complexity.

title: Non-interactive Element in Tab Order
desc: A non-interactive element (such as a div, paragraph, or progress bar) is in the tab order. Keyboard users tab to it but cannot do anything with it, which is confusing.
rem: Remove the tabindex attribute from non-interactive elements. Only native interactive elements or elements that need programmatic focus (such as dialog headings) should receive focus.

title: Repeated Links to the Same Destination
desc: A content block has multiple separate links or buttons that all go to the same place — for example, a card with a linked image, a linked title, and a "Read more" button. Keyboard users must tab through all of them, and screen reader users hear repeated announcements.
rem: Combine them into a single link. Mark the image as decorative (alt="") and use the text as the link label. Or wrap the entire card in one link element.

title: Language Change Not Marked in HTML
desc: The page contains text in more than one language, but the language change is not marked in the HTML. Screen readers may read foreign words using the wrong pronunciation.
rem: Add a lang attribute to the element wrapping the text in a different language. For example: Hola.

title: Page Language Not Set
desc: The html element has no lang attribute. Screen readers may use the wrong language profile to read the page, causing incorrect pronunciation.
rem: Add a lang attribute to the html element that matches the primary language of the page. For example: <html lang="en">.

title: Drag Action Has No Keyboard Alternative
desc: A feature requires the user to drag an element with a pointer. There is no keyboard-accessible way to perform the same action.
rem: Provide keyboard-accessible controls (such as buttons) that perform the same action as dragging. Keyboard users should be able to complete every task without a mouse.

title: Looping Animation Cannot Be Paused
desc: An animation or moving element starts automatically and loops without stopping. There is no way for the user to pause, stop, or hide it. This can be distracting or harmful for people with certain conditions.
rem: Provide a visible, keyboard-accessible button to pause or stop the animation. Or set it to stop automatically within 5 seconds. If the animation conveys live data (like a news ticker), a pause button is required.

title: Page Landmarks Missing or Incorrect
desc: Page content is not organized inside HTML landmark elements. Screen reader users cannot jump between sections of the page — they must read everything from the start.
rem: Wrap all page content in semantic HTML elements: header, nav, main, aside, and footer. Every page needs at least one main element. Use ARIA landmark roles only when the right HTML element is not available.

title: Page Title Does Not Change Between Pages
desc: The page title (shown in the browser tab) stays the same on all pages. Users cannot tell which page they are on from the tab alone.
rem: Update the document title on each page to describe what that page is about. For example: "Cart — My Store" or "Settings — App Name". In a single-page app, update the title on each route change.

title: Keyboard Trap
desc: Keyboard focus gets stuck inside a component. Once a keyboard user tabs into it, there is no way out using only the keyboard.
rem: Make sure keyboard users can always tab out of any component. If a modal or dialog traps focus intentionally, add an Escape key handler and a visible close button so users can leave.

title: Chart or Graph Has No Text Alternative
desc: Charts and graphs convey data visually but have no text alternative. Screen reader users cannot access the information the chart contains.
rem: Provide a text summary that describes what the chart shows — its type, key trends, and main takeaways. When possible, also provide the underlying data in a table.

title: Table Data Not Using Table Markup
desc: Data organized in rows and columns is not using HTML table markup. Screen reader users cannot understand the relationship between column headers and data cells.
rem: Use proper table markup with table, thead, tbody, tr, th, and td elements. Make sure column and row headers use th elements with appropriate scope attributes.

title: Tooltip or Hover Content Not Keyboard Accessible
scLabel: 1.4.13 Content on Hover or Focus (Level AA)
desc: Extra content appears only when the user hovers with a mouse. Keyboard users and screen reader users cannot trigger or read this content.
rem: Make hover content also appear when the element receives keyboard focus. Users must be able to dismiss it without moving focus (for example, with Escape). The content should stay visible until the user moves focus away.

title: Tab Order Does Not Match Visual Order
desc: When tabbing through the page, focus jumps in an order that does not match what is shown on screen. This is confusing for keyboard users.
rem: Make the HTML source order match the visual layout. Avoid using positive tabindex values to control tab order — they create maintenance problems and usually make things worse.

title: Informative Content Hidden from Screen Readers
desc: Content that carries meaning (like a star rating or status icon) is hidden from screen readers using aria-hidden. Screen reader users cannot access that information.
rem: Remove aria-hidden from content that carries meaning. Add an accessible name or supplemental text that conveys the same information. For example, instead of hiding a star rating, add hidden text like "Rating: 4 out of 5 stars".

title: No Warning Before Opening a New Window
desc: A link or button opens a new browser window or tab without warning. This is disorienting, especially for screen reader users who may not realize the context has changed.
rem: Add a warning in the link text or accessible name. For example: "Annual Report (opens in a new tab)". You can also add an icon with alt text to indicate a new window will open.

title: Receiving Focus Causes Unexpected Change
desc: When an element receives keyboard or pointer focus, the page changes — for example, a form submits or a new page loads. This is unexpected and disorienting.
rem: Do not trigger any actions when an element receives focus. Actions should only happen when the user deliberately activates a control (for example, by pressing Enter, Space, or clicking).

title: Changing an Input Causes Unexpected Change
desc: Selecting an option in a dropdown or changing a form value automatically causes the page to reload or navigate. Users who keyboard through a list of options may trigger an unintended change.
rem: Do not trigger page-level changes when the user changes a form value. Instead, wait for a deliberate submit action — like pressing a "Go" button — before acting on the selection.

title: Content Announced Incorrectly by Screen Readers
desc: Content is formatted in a way that causes screen readers to read it incorrectly. For example, a price of "$1,200" may be read as garbled text depending on how it is marked up.
rem: Review how the content is structured in the HTML and test with a screen reader. Fix the markup or formatting so the announced text conveys the intended meaning accurately.

title: Figure or Illustration Has No Description
desc: An image or diagram uses a figure element but has no figcaption or accessible description. Screen reader users hear the image file name or a generic announcement instead of what the image shows.
rem: Add a figcaption element inside the figure that explains what the image shows or why it matters. For more complex visuals, link to a longer text description nearby.

title: Form Field Has Conflicting Labels
desc: A form field has both a visible label and an aria-label that say different things. Screen reader users hear the aria-label while sighted users read the visible label, which creates confusion.
rem: Use only one labeling method, or make sure both labels say the same thing. The accessible name (aria-label or aria-labelledby) must contain the visible label text.

title: Dropdown or Select Has No Label
desc: A dropdown menu or select element has no label. Screen reader users do not know what choice they are making.
rem: Add a visible label element with a for attribute that matches the select element's id. If you cannot show a visible label, use aria-label or aria-labelledby instead.

title: Layout Breaks When Text Is Enlarged
desc: When users increase text size in their browser to 200%, the page layout breaks. Text overlaps other content, gets cut off, or disappears. Low vision users who rely on larger text cannot read the page.
rem: Use flexible layouts and relative units (rem, em, %) instead of fixed pixel heights. Test the page at 200% text size in your browser settings to make sure everything remains readable and nothing overflows.

title: Vague or Generic Link Text
desc: Links use generic text like "Click here", "Read more", or "Learn more". Screen reader users who navigate by links cannot tell where each link goes.
rem: Write link text that describes the destination or action. Instead of "Click here", use "Download the accessibility checklist" or "Read the full WCAG 1.1.1 explanation".

title: Audio or Video Has No Transcript or Captions
desc: A video or audio recording has no captions or transcript. Deaf and hard of hearing users cannot access the spoken content.
rem: For audio-only content, provide a full text transcript. For video with audio, provide synchronized captions. Place the transcript near the media or link to it clearly. Auto-generated captions must be reviewed and corrected before publishing.

title: Form Group Has No Group Label
desc: A group of related form controls (like radio buttons or checkboxes) has no group label. Screen reader users hear each option without understanding what question it answers.
rem: Wrap the group in a fieldset element and add a legend as its first child. The legend text should be the question or category the group belongs to. For example: "Choose your preferred contact method".

title: List Content Not Using List Markup
desc: Content that looks like a list — such as navigation links, steps, or options — is built with divs or paragraphs instead of HTML list elements. Screen readers cannot announce how many items are in the list.
rem: Use ul for unordered lists, ol for numbered lists, and dl for definition-style lists. Pair each list with li or dt/dd items. This also helps with navigation menus and step-by-step instructions.

title: Live Region Not Announcing Updates
desc: Content that updates dynamically — like a search result count, a progress update, or a notification — is not announced by screen readers because the live region is missing or set up incorrectly.
rem: Add aria-live="polite" to a container that will receive the updated text. Use aria-live="assertive" only for urgent alerts. Inject the message into the live region after it is already in the DOM — injecting the region and message at the same time may not be announced.

title: Multi-Point Gesture Has No Single-Pointer Alternative
desc: A feature requires a multi-finger gesture — like pinch-to-zoom or a two-finger swipe — with no single-tap or keyboard alternative. Users with motor disabilities who cannot perform multi-touch gestures are locked out.
rem: Provide a single-pointer alternative for every multi-point gesture. For example, add plus and minus zoom buttons alongside pinch-to-zoom. All gestures must have a keyboard-accessible equivalent.

title: Error Message Does Not Explain How to Fix the Problem
desc: A form shows an error when the user submits, but the message does not say how to fix it. For example, it may say "Invalid input" without explaining what format is expected.
rem: Write specific, actionable error messages. Tell users exactly what went wrong and how to correct it. For example: "Phone number must be 10 digits, numbers only" instead of "Invalid phone number".

title: Video Has No Closed Captions
desc: A prerecorded video has spoken audio but no captions. Deaf and hard of hearing users cannot access the spoken content, and users watching in noisy or sound-sensitive environments cannot follow along.
rem: Add accurate captions to every prerecorded video that has a spoken audio track. Captions must be synchronized with the audio, include speaker identification where relevant, and describe important non-speech sounds (like [applause] or [doorbell]). Review auto-generated captions for accuracy before publishing.

title: Video Has No Audio Description
desc: A prerecorded video contains visual information that is not described in the audio — such as on-screen text, actions, or diagrams. Blind and low vision users miss this content entirely.
rem: Add an audio description track that narrates key visual content during natural pauses in the dialogue. If there are not enough pauses, create an extended audio description version with the video paused at relevant moments. An alternative is a full text description, but an audio track is preferred.
